food.text: Iraqi food changes as you travel through the country. In Northern Iraq, pomegranate is added to dolma, while in Southern Iraq fish is a staple. The center of the country is known for its rice dishes and sweets.

Lower Mesopotamia grows rice, barley and citrus fruits. It is also responsible for Iraq's position as one of the world's largest producers of dates. Iraqi farming still harks back to ancient Mesopotamia.

Levantine cuisine is particularly known for its meze spreads of hot and cold dishes, always accompanied by bread. Among the best known are manakish pies, kibbeh, ful medames, hummus, tabbouleh and baba ghanoush.

Masgouf is a traditional Mesopotamian dish made with fish from the Tigris. The open-cut freshwater fish is marinated with olive oil, salt, curcuma and tamarind, then roasted for hours with the skin on. It is garnished with lemon, chopped onions and tomatoes, and clay-oven flatbreads.

Mouneh is the Levantine practice of preserving seasonal foods for times of scarcity, including syrups, jams, dried foods and pickles. Brining in salt is traditionally a primary method, and meats were traditionally preserved in fat. The Oxford Companion to Food described Syria and Lebanon as having "a strong culture of preserving seasonal foods". Such foods were traditionally made to ensure food security, and mouneh was used to cope with wars, like the Syrian civil war.

The western Syrian part of Upper Mesopotamia is essentially contiguous with the al-Hasakah Governorate and is described as "Syria's breadbasket". The region lies between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, and the Khabur runs across its plain.

Long-grain rice is a staple in Iraqi cuisine, cooked in a multistep process meant to produce just-tender, fluffy grains. Prized is the hikakeh, a crisp bottom crust. Before serving, it is broken into pieces so everyone gets some along with the rice.

Karabeej Halab, meaning 'Whips of Aleppo', is a churro-like fried dough made with semolina flour. After deep frying it is dipped into a sugar and rose water syrup. It originates from Syrian cuisine and is also common in Jordan and the West Bank, especially during Ramadan.

Zardah is a sweet rice dessert used on religious occasions such as Ramadan and Eid. It is made of soaked rice with a sticky, jelly-like consistency, with sugar and yellow tea dye added. It is decorated with cinnamon, coconut and nuts.

Pork consumption is forbidden to Muslims in Iraq, in accordance with Sharia, the Islamic law. Iraqi stews instead centre on foods like fasolia yabsa, a white bean stew of tender lamb or veal, white kidney beans and tomato sauce served over rice.

The 1949 introduction of rationing boosted falafel's popularity in Israel. It was a good source of protein and its ingredients were easily available to everybody. The dish had first reached Mandatory Palestine, where some Jews and Arabs adopted it, though many recent Ashkenazi Jewish migrants were hesitant.
Freekeh is a Levantine cereal food made from green durum wheat that is roasted and rubbed to create its flavour. It is served with cumin, cinnamon, and fresh lamb-tail fat.
Ful medames, made from ground fava beans and olive oil, is also prepared in Syria as a salad. That version adds chopped tomatoes, onion, parsley, lemon juice, pepper and salt.

art.text: Between 1899 and 1914, German archaeologist Robert Koldewey directed the excavation of Babylon, with more than 200 people working daily, year round, for fifteen years. When his team unearthed the Processional street in 1899, the modern world got its first look at the site of this much-storied city.

In the 20th century, an art revival in Iraq produced many notable poets, painters and sculptors who contributed to the inventory of public artworks, especially in Baghdad. Poetry remains a major art form in modern Iraq, and poets living in exile often wrote about 'strangeness' and 'being a stranger'.

Between 1922 and 1934, Leonard Woolley led excavations at Ur for the University of Pennsylvania Museum and the British Museum. The Royal Cemetery yielded many art discoveries, including the twin 'Rams in a Thicket', and Woolley documented the work in ten volumes of Ur Excavations in 1927.

The Lyres of Ur are considered the world's oldest surviving stringed instruments. In 1929, archaeologists led by Leonard Woolley discovered pieces of three lyres and one harp at the Royal Cemetery of Ur, in what is now Iraq. They are over 4,500 years old.

Koldewey's digs at Babylon revealed the foundations of the ziggurat and the Ishtar Gate. He also developed a method to identify and excavate mud brick architecture, which proved especially useful for the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, built mainly of unfired mudbricks.

The Baghdad Modern Art Group sought to express modern life while keeping tradition and heritage in perspective, which distinguished it from earlier art groups. Members included Nuri al-Rawi, who became the Minister for Culture, and Mohammed Ghani Hikmat.

In 1929, Leonard Woolley's archaeologists discovered the Lyres of Ur in the Royal Cemetery, considered the world's oldest surviving stringed instruments. They found pieces of three lyres and one harp, over 4,500 years old, whose decorations are fine examples of Mesopotamian court art.

The Great Ziggurat of Ur was excavated in the 1920s and 1930s by teams led by Leonard Woolley. In the 1980s, Saddam Hussein ordered the façade of its lowest level and its monumental staircase rebuilt, encasing the ancient remains.

Walter Andrae, a participant in the Babylon expedition, later created models of the city for the Vorderasiatisches Museum Berlin. The excavations were considered prestigious for Germany, and so were well sponsored and well publicized.

The Baghdad Modern Art Group was moribund within a decade of its formation. Co-founder Jawad Saleem died in 1961, while the other co-founder, Shakir Hassan Al Said, suffered a mental and spiritual crisis amid the turbulence following the 1958 revolution and the overthrow of the Hashemite monarchy.
Madiha Omar (1908–2005) is regarded as a pioneer of the Hurufiyya movement. She is listed among the notable Iraqi artists of the 20th century, alongside Shakir Hassan Al Said and Rafa al-Nasiri.

The rebuilt Ziggurat of Ur was damaged in the Gulf War in 1991 by small arms fire, and the structure was shaken by explosions. Four bomb craters can be seen nearby, and its walls are marred by over 400 bullet holes.

war.text: Ba'athist Syria's covert chemical weapons program began in the 1970s with assistance from Egypt and the Soviet Union. During the Syrian civil war, sarin and chlorine were used in hundreds of attacks, most of them attributed to the Syrian Arab Armed Forces.
war.source_title: Syria and weapons of mass destruction

war.text: The Mesopotamian campaign of World War I began after the British Fao Landing in 1914. Britain sought to protect Anglo-Persian Oil Company oil fields in Khuzestan province and the Shatt al-Arab waterway. The fighting was against the Ottoman Empire, and most British Empire troops came from the British Raj.

World War I saw the first large-scale use of machine guns, artillery, aircraft, chemical weapons and tanks. It lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918 and caused an estimated 15 to 22 million deaths, including those in war crimes and genocides, and it helped spread the Spanish flu pandemic. Germany first used chlorine gas on the Western Front on 22 April 1915, at the Second Battle of Ypres, in violation of the Hague Convention. Meanwhile, the Ottoman Empire conducted large-scale ethnic cleansing of Armenian, Greek and Assyrian Christians, the Armenian, Greek and Assyrian genocides, while the British opened the Mesopotamian campaign in 1914.

On 26 February 1991, US and British armored forces fought Iraq's Republican Guard at the Battle of 73 Easting, which one participant called "the last great tank battle of the 20th century." It was named for a north–south coordinate line that Coalition forces used to measure their progress through the desert.

The British advance up the Tigris and Euphrates stalled at the town of Kut in December 1915. In the Siege of Kut, which began on 7 December, the garrison could be defended but not resupplied. Air drops were not enough to feed it, disease spread rapidly and could not be cured, and several British attempts to break through failed at heavy cost, with high casualties on both sides. Townshend surrendered on 29 April 1916 and 13,164 soldiers became Ottoman captives, a defeat later called "the worst defeat of the Allies in World War I". The British then re-organised and began a new campaign to take Baghdad.

After the defeat at Kut, British Imperial forces reorganised and captured Baghdad in March 1917. The British were aided in Mesopotamia by local Arab and Assyrian fighters. The Ottomans, by contrast, employed local Kurdish and Turcoman tribes.

Churchill authorised a shipment of artillery shells containing ethyl iodoacetate, a tear gas, from Egypt to Iraq on 17 September 1920. Trials on British soldiers showed that the large quantity of shells needed to produce a significant irritant effect was logistically impractical.
war.source_title: Alleged British use of chemical weapons in the Iraqi Revolt

war.text: In May 1969 the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine attacked and damaged the Trans-Arabian Pipeline. The strike spilled tons of oil into the Sea of Galilee and cost both Aramco and the Saudi government significant revenue.
tags: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine

war.text: The Armistice of Mudros was signed on 30 October 1918, with both sides remaining in position. General Cobbe did not stand fast as the armistice required, and continued to advance on Mosul despite Turkish protests. British troops marched unopposed into the city on 14 November 1918.
The war in Mesopotamia ended on 14 November 1918, fifteen days after the Armistice of Mudros. Ownership of Mosul Province and its rich oil fields then became an international issue.

On 9 January 1922 Churchill approved converting gas artillery shells for use from aircraft, as the air force remained enthusiastic about gas. He halted the plan on 31 January under pressure from the Air Council. The Washington Disarmament Treaty, signed on 7 January 1922, had prohibited the use of "asphyxiating, poisonous or other gases".
war.source_title: Alleged British use of chemical weapons in the Iraqi Revolt

war.text: On 26 February 1991, a British Army Challenger 1 destroyed an Iraqi T-55 at a range of 4.7 km (2.9 miles) with an HESH round. This was the longest tank-to-tank kill in military history.

In March 1918, Britain faced an uprising by a rebel organisation called Jam'iya al-Nahda al-Islamiya in Najaf. British forces laid siege to the city until May, when the rebels surrendered. It happened while the British were still fighting the Ottomans elsewhere in Mesopotamia.

In summer 1918 General Marshall moved some of his forces east in support of Dunsterforce, led by General Lionel Dunsterville, in Persia. British troops were also moved to the Sinai and Palestine Campaign in support of the Battle of Megiddo. His very powerful army was described as "astonishingly inactive" for most of the period.

Contradictory claims about gas in Iraq were partly the product of an inaccurate September 1921 letter by J. A. Webster of the Air Ministry. It claimed poison gas shells had already been used by the army during the previous year's rebellion. In December 1921 the Air Ministry revised its position, stating that it was not known whether gas shells were used.
war.source_title: Alleged British use of chemical weapons in the Iraqi Revolt

literature.text: Psalm 137 begins "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down" and laments exile during the Babylonian captivity. It ends with prophetic predictions of violent revenge, a call for violence against children. Leonard Cohen referred to the psalm several times in his song and poem "By the Rivers Dark", which appears on his 2001 album Ten New Songs and in his 2006 poetry collection Book of Longing.

Arthur C. Clarke wrote a short story called "If I Forget Thee, Oh Earth", first published in 1951 in the magazine Future. It is listed among the modern works that draw on Psalm 137, the lament of exiles who yearn for Jerusalem while dwelling in the Babylonian captivity. That lament ends with a call for violence against children and violent revenge on the exiles' enemies.
tags: If I Forget Thee, Oh Earth

literature.text: In early April 2003 Iraq's museum was looted after the US invasion of Baghdad. The gold-and-mother-of-pearl bull's head lyre from Ur went missing and was found in pieces: the irreparably damaged bull's head turned up in the flooded basement vaults of Iraq's Central Bank, while looters had stripped much of the gold from the body and left the remains in a parking lot. At a 2016 event in London's Trafalgar Square condemning ISIS and the looting, Stef Conner and Mark Hamer played a replica of the lyre, performing a musical interpretation of The Epic of Gilgamesh from their 2014 album The Flood.

Elizabeth Goudge used the opening words of Psalm 137 as the title of a short story, By the Waters of Babylon. It follows an Egyptian slave girl who meets Mary and Joseph shortly after the Nativity and warns them about King Herod. It was published in The Ikon on the Wall, and Other Stories in 1943.

The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (ETCSL) is a University of Oxford project that gathers nearly 400 literary compositions from ancient Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq. Its texts date to the late third and early second millennia BCE, and the project now puts them within reach of modern readers.
Nazik Al-Malaika (1923–2007) became one of the best known woman poets in the Arab world. She wrote the poem My Brother Jafaar for her brother, who was killed during the Al-Wathbah uprising in 1948.

Two of the surviving decrees of Urukagina, an early Mesopotamian ruler, were first published and translated by Samuel Kramer in 1964. One seems to have abolished polyandry, on pain of the woman who took multiple husbands being stoned with rocks upon which her crime was written. Another states that if a woman says [text illegible] to a man, her mouth is crushed with burnt bricks. No comparable penalties for adultery by men have survived, so some modern critics call the decrees "the first written evidence of the degradation of women."

The Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI), published from 1998 to 2022, presents images of cuneiform tablets online for the non-commercial use of students, scholars and the public. Its support came from bodies including the Mellon Foundation and the Max Planck Society, and it works alongside the Sumerian literature corpus at Oxford.

The Pennsylvania Sumerian Dictionary (PSD) is carried out in the Babylonian Section of the University of Pennsylvania Museum of Anthropology and Archaeology. Published from 2003 to 2022, it is funded by the NEH and private contributions. It works with other projects such as the CDLI and the ETCSL to develop tools for reading Sumerian texts.

science.text: The Iraq Petroleum Company built a pipeline from Kirkuk to the Mediterranean coast between the summer of 1932 and 1934. Oil first reached Tripoli on July 14, 1934, and Haifa on October 14, 1934, exactly seven years after oil was first struck at the Baba Gurgur No. 1 well.

Construction of the Trans-Arabian Pipeline, carrying oil from Qaisumah in Saudi Arabia to Sidon in Lebanon, began in 1947 under the American company Bechtel. Consolidated Steel of Los Angeles supplied 980 miles of 30 and 31 inch pipe, while the National Tube Company of Pittsburgh supplied another 70 miles.

In March 2014, as part of a cooperation project between Italy's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Iraq's State Board of Antiquities and Heritage, a UAV was flown over the ancient city of Ur. The flight produced the first high-resolution aerial map of the site, built from more than 100 photographs with an accuracy of 20 centimeters or less.
tags: State Board of Antiquities and Heritage

science.text: The Kirkuk oilfield was discovered by the Turkish Petroleum Company at Baba Gurgur in 1927. It was brought into production by the Iraq Petroleum Company in 1934, once twin 12-inch pipelines from Kirkuk to Haifa and Tripoli were completed.

The Iraq Petroleum Company added a 16-inch loop to its Kirkuk-Haifa pipeline in 1948 and 1949, raising its capacity to 250,000 barrels per day. After finishing the Tapline project, Bechtel built the Iraq pipeline a further 30-inch loop with a capacity of 300,000 barrels per day, completed in April 1952.

By 1998 the Kirkuk oilfield held over 10 billion barrels of proven remaining oil reserves. After about seven decades of operation it was still producing up to 1 million barrels per day, almost half of all Iraqi oil exports.

Archaeologists discovered a new gate at Nineveh in 2021, north of the Shamash Gate, next to a water tunnel running 42 meters beneath the city's 31-meter-thick wall, an area excavated in 2020 and 2021. Geophysical surveys were also carried out north of Tell Kuyunjiq in 2021 and 2023 ahead of further research.

Some analysts believe poor reservoir-management practices during the Saddam Hussein years permanently damaged the Kirkuk oilfield. An estimated 1.5 billion barrels of excess fuel oil were reinjected into the field, increasing oil viscosity and making it harder and more costly to extract.

politics.text: The Mesopotamian campaign of World War I pitted the British Empire, using mostly troops from the British Raj, against the Ottoman Empire for control of Ottoman Iraq. It began with the British Fao Landing in 1914, meant to protect Anglo-Persian Oil Company oil fields. It ended with the Armistice of Mudros in 1918, leading to the cession of Iraq and further partition of the Ottoman Empire.

After World War I, the lands of present-day eastern Syria were placed under Iraqi-British administration. Iraq ultimately and irrevocably lost these territories over the course of the 20th century. The French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon placed the western part of Upper Mesopotamia inside the boundaries of the modern Syrian state, separating the western Jazira from Iraq.

Thousands of Assyrian refugees entered Syria's Jazira province from Turkey following the Assyrian genocide of World War I. In 1933 a further 24,000 Assyrian Christians fled into the area after the Simele massacre in the Mosul region of northern Iraq. The article notes that violence against Christians changed the demographics of Upper Mesopotamia, and that Demographics in the region shifted hugely in the first half of the 20th century.

On 14 November 1914 the Ottoman government declared a holy war, or jihad, against the enemies of Islam, excluding the Central Powers. This swayed some Ottoman Arabs to stay loyal to the empire and fight the Allied Powers. Among them were some Shia Muslims, previously an oppressed group within the empire.

In 1919, Arab forces associated with Faisal's government in Damascus occupied Zor, the administrative center of Upper Mesopotamia, placing it under the authority of the Arab government in Syria. French forces defeated and expelled Faisal's government in July 1920. This brought these territories under French colonial administration.

In September 2013 the United States, Russia and Syria agreed to eliminate Syria's declared chemical weapon stockpile, excluding chlorine. The OPCW-UN Joint Mission finished destroying Syria's declared production facilities by the end of October 2013 and shipped the stockpile overseas by June 2014.
politics.source_title: Syria and weapons of mass destruction

politics.text: In March 1918, Britain faced an uprising in Najaf by a rebel organisation called Jam'iya al-Nahda al-Islamiya. British forces laid siege to the city until May, when the rebels surrendered. Later that year, troops were also moved to the Sinai and Palestine Campaign and to Persia.

philosophy.text: The term "Abrahamic religions" was introduced in the 20th century. It replaced "Judeo-Christian" so that Islam could be included and the differences between Judaism and Christianity acknowledged. Some scholars have criticized the term.

Panbabylonism was a school of thought founded by Hugo Winckler and held in the early 20th century, mostly by German Assyriologists. It claimed a common cultural system across the ancient Near East, overwhelmingly shaped by the Babylonians. It even held that the Hebrew Bible and Judaism were rooted in Babylonian astral science.

The ancient Liturgy of Addai and Mari, used in the Assyrian churches, long blocked ecumenism because its anaphora lacks the Words of Institution, which the Catholic Church sees as indispensable. In 2001 the Catholic Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith determined the text could be considered valid in Catholicism as well.

The theory of a Babylonian-derived Bible grew out of the discovery of a stele in the acropolis of Susa. It bore a Babylonian flood myth with many similarities to the flood of Genesis. Critics noted that flood myths appear in almost every culture, including ones that never had contact with Mesopotamia.

Alexander Hislop's 1853 book The Two Babylons drew on Panbabylonian ideas, arguing that the Catholic Church continued the religion of ancient Babylon. Twentieth-century scholars relegated Panbabylonism to pseudohistory. Yet in 1921 A. W. Pink claimed the book had proven its case conclusively, and The Watchtower published excerpts until the 1980s.

The fundamental tenets of Panbabylonism were eventually dismissed as pseudoscientific. Even so, Assyriologists and biblical scholars recognize an indirect influence of Babylonian mythology on Jewish mythology and other Near Eastern mythologies. The similarities between the traditions may also draw on even older sources.

The inscribed tablets found since 1928 at the Canaanite city of Ugarit, destroyed around 1200 BCE, have not revealed a cosmology. Modern archaeology has transformed knowledge of Canaanite religion, yet the picture remains fragmentary and insufficient for a complete and continuous account.

culture.text: The Assyrian people survive to this day and still live and practice their culture in their ancient heartland in Upper Mesopotamia, which was the base of a civilization that existed from the 21st to the 7th century BCE. Survival came at great cost. Religiously motivated suppression and massacres under the Ilkhanate and the Timurid Empire in the 14th century reduced them to a local ethnic and religious minority. In the late 19th and early 20th century, Ottoman persecutions and massacres culminated in the Sayfo (Assyrian genocide), which killed as many as 250,000 Assyrians. Further massacres and persecutions, by governments and by terrorist groups such as the Islamic State, have left most Assyrians living in diaspora.

Approximately 95% to 98% of Iraqis are Muslim, with Shia around 55% and Sunnis around 40%. Although Iraq is an Arab country in the Arab world, its geopolitical history with Iran has meant that it is majority Shia.

Zoroastrianism, arguably the world's oldest monotheistic religion, almost disappeared in the last century. Many Kurds converted from Islam to Zoroastrianism after ISIL attacked Iraqi Kurdistan, which the article largely attributes to disillusionment with Islam after years of violence and barbarism by the ISIS terrorist group. A Kurdish Islamic cleric claimed Zoroastrianism was forced on Kurds by "fire-worshipping Persians" and called on Kurdish Muslims to kill Zoroastrian converts who did not convert back to Islam in 3 days. As of August 2015 the Kurdistan Regional Government officially recognized it as a religion within Kurdish Iraq.

After the failed Kurdish rebellions in Kemalist Turkey in the mid-1920s, an estimated 25,000 Kurds fled to northern Syria under French Mandate authorities to escape the subsequent Turkish onslaught. The authorities encouraged their immigration and granted them Syrian citizenship. Another wave of refugees arrived in 1929.

The term "Uruk period" was coined at a conference in Baghdad in 1930. It drew on earlier excavations and on the first discoveries made by German archaeologists in Uruk in 1929, and Uruk-period levels were fully excavated in the 1950s and 1960s.

Iraq's Baháʼí community became increasingly institutionalized in the 20th century. The government permitted an Iraqi Baháʼí National Spiritual Assembly in 1931, recognized Baháʼí marriages in 1947, and counted Baháʼís in the 1957 census. In 1970 the Ba'athist government prohibited Baháʼí activity, expropriated Baháʼí property, imprisoned adherents and prohibited Baháʼí religious literature. Federal Iraqi law still prohibits the practice of the faith, although the ban is generally not enforced.

French official reports show 45 Kurdish villages in Syria's Jazira province before 1927. As the mandatory authorities continued to encourage Kurdish immigration, the villages numbered between 700 and 800 by 1939.

Efforts have also been made to approach reunification of the Assyrian and Chaldean churches. In 1996, Dinkha IV and Patriarch Raphael I Bidawid of the Chaldean Church signed a list of common proposals to move toward unity, approved by synods of both churches in 1997.

In March 2020, archaeologists announced the discovery of a 5,000-year-old cultic area at Girsu, filled with more than 300 broken ceremonial cups, bowls and jars, plus animal bones. It was dedicated to Ningirsu, and a duck-shaped bronze figurine with bark eyes is thought to be dedicated to Nanshe.

According to Yasna, an association promoting Zoroastrianism in Kurdistan, about 15,000 people have registered since 2014, most of them Kurds converting from Islam. Many converted especially after ISIL attacked Iraqi Kurdistan, and the surge is largely attributed to disillusionment with Islam after years of violence and barbarism by the ISIS terrorist group. The first new Zoroastrian temples were built and opened in 2016.

French geographers Fevret and Gibert estimated that in 1953 Jazira had 146,000 inhabitants. Agriculturalist Kurds made up 60,000 (41%), nomad Arabs 50,000 (34%), and a quarter of the population were Christians.

In 2023, Iraq scored 1 out of 4 for religious freedom. This indicates a supposed lack of religious freedom enforced by the state, in a country whose religious life has ancient Mesopotamian, Persian, Arab and Judeo-Christian influences.
